prompt: Compare per-image billing with token billing for a pipeline that generates 20,000 product images per month. Give a decision rule in three bullet points.
response:
## The structural difference

| | Per-image billing | Token billing |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of charge | One output image at a quality/size tier | Input tokens (prompt + reference images + history) + output tokens (image) |
| Cost of a long prompt | Free | Charged |
| Cost of reference images / multi-turn edits | Free | Charged every call, and grows if you resend conversation history |
| Cost of small or odd-sized outputs | Usually rounded up to the nearest tier | Scales with actual image tokens |
| Retries and rejects | Full price each | Full price each |
| Caching discounts | Rarely available | Often available on repeated system prompts/references |
| Forecastability | High (one number × volume) | Medium (depends on prompt shape) |

Key insight: for most image models, output image tokens are effectively **fixed per resolution tier**, so token billing behaves like per-image billing *plus a variable input surcharge*. The decision therefore usually turns on how heavy your input side is, not on your output volume.

## Break-even math at 20,000 images/month

Let `P` = per-image price, `O` = output tokens/image × output rate, `I` = input tokens/call, `r_i` = input rate.

**Token billing wins when `I < (P − O) / r_i`.**

Illustrative (verify current vendor rates — these move):

- **Baseline:** 20,000 × $0.04 = **$800/mo**. A comparable token path at ~1,300 output tokens × $30/M ≈ $0.039/image plus a 200-token prompt (~$0.0005) ≈ **$790/mo**. Effectively a tie.
- **Retry reality:** if you generate 1.4 images per accepted image, both jump to ~28,000 calls ≈ **$1,100/mo**. Always price per *accepted* image, not per call.
- **Input-heavy case:** 3 reference images (~1,100 tokens each) + 4-turn edit loop with resent history → input can reach 10k–15k tokens/call, adding **$500–$1,000/mo** on the token path only.
- **Small-output case:** if half your volume is 512px variants, token billing bills roughly proportionally while per-image tiers often charge the full 1K price — token billing can save 20–30% on that slice.

Also worth noting at this volume: 20k/month is only ~27 images/hour, so if generation isn't user-facing, an async/batch tier (commonly ~50% off) will beat *any* optimization between the two billing models. And $800–$4,000/mo is typically below the threshold where committed-use discounts are offered, so don't assume negotiation will change the ranking.

## Decision rule

- **Compute effective cost per *accepted* image under both models using your actual prompt and retry profile; if the gap is under ~15%, take per-image billing** — the forecasting simplicity and clean COGS-per-SKU attribution is worth more than a marginal saving at 20k/month.
- **Choose token billing if your pipeline is input-light and output-variable:** short templated prompts, no or few reference images, single-shot generation, mixed/small resolutions, and a cacheable system prompt.
- **Choose per-image billing if your pipeline is input-heavy or variance-intolerant:** multi-reference conditioning, multi-turn editing loops, long prompts, or a need to quote a fixed unit cost to finance or to customers — because token cost scales with context you can't fully control.

prompt: Write a six-step checklist for moving an OpenAI-compatible workload from one API gateway to another, including rollback.
response:
# Migration Checklist: OpenAI-Compatible Workload → New API Gateway

## 1. Inventory the surface you actually depend on

"OpenAI-compatible" is a spectrum, and gateways diverge at the edges.

- **Endpoints in use:** `/chat/completions`, `/responses`, `/embeddings`, `/models`, `/audio/*`, `/images/*`, `/batches`, `/files`.
- **Request params:** `tools` / `tool_choice`, `response_format` (especially `json_schema` strictness), `stream_options.include_usage`, `seed`, `logprobs`, `n`, `stop`, `logit_bias`, `max_tokens` vs `max_completion_tokens`, `reasoning_effort`.
- **Response shape:** SSE chunk framing and `[DONE]` sentinel, `finish_reason` values, `usage` field presence/placement, tool-call ID formats, `refusal` field, multi-part content arrays.
- **Error contract:** HTTP codes, JSON error body shape (`error.type`/`error.code`), `Retry-After` and rate-limit headers your client retry logic reads.
- **Headers & auth:** `Authorization`, `OpenAI-Organization`/`Project`, custom routing headers, idempotency keys.
- **Operational limits:** max body size, request timeout, context window per model, concurrency and TPM/RPM quotas.

> **Exit gate:** a written compatibility matrix with every gap labeled *blocking*, *shimmable*, or *ignorable*.

## 2. Stand up the target gateway as configuration, not code

- Map model names explicitly (`gpt-4o-2024-11-20` → target alias); **pin versions**, avoid floating aliases during migration.
- Provision credentials, quotas, rate limits, caching, guardrails, and log redaction policies.
- Clear the network path: egress allowlists, private link/VPC peering, mTLS, proxy chains, TLS cert trust.
- Ensure `base_url`, model name, API key, and timeouts are **runtime-configurable** (env/flag/config service) — no rebuild required to switch or revert.
- Write shims for *shimmable* gaps from Step 1 behind a single adapter layer.

> **Exit gate:** one config change flips a client between gateways, in both directions.

## 3. Prove parity offline before any production traffic

- Replay a **golden corpus** (200–1000 real, de-identified requests) against old and new gateways; include long contexts, multimodal inputs, tool-calling loops, and JSON-schema outputs.
- Diff **structurally**, not byte-exact: schema validity, tool-call arity and argument parseability, `finish_reason` distribution, token-count drift, empty/refusal rate.
- Compare **streaming** chunk-by-chunk: first-token latency, chunk cadence, usage delivery, mid-stream error behavior.
- Inject failures: 401, 404 model, 429, 500, timeout, context-length overflow, canceled stream — confirm your client retry/backoff still behaves.
- Load-test to expected peak: TTFT, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end, tokens/sec, error rate, cost per 1K requests.

> **Exit gate:** documented pass/fail thresholds met; unresolved *blocking* gaps = stop.

## 4. Build and rehearse rollback **before** cutover

- Keep the old gateway **hot** — credentials valid, quotas reserved, capacity unscaled-down, for the entire rollback window.
- Define the rollback mechanism and measure it: feature flag or config push (seconds, preferred) over DNS/TTL changes (minutes, fragile).
- Handle **stateful residue**: in-flight batch jobs, uploaded files, server-side conversation/thread state, vector stores, prompt caches, gateway-side semantic cache. These usually *do not* migrate — drain or dual-write, never assume.
- Write explicit rollback triggers with owners and no-debate authority:

| Trigger | Threshold |
|---|---|
| 5xx / gateway error rate | > 1% over 5 min |
| p95 latency or TTFT | > 1.5× baseline over 10 min |
| Malformed tool calls / schema failures | > 0.5% |
| Empty or refusal responses | > 2× baseline |
| Cost per request | > 1.3× baseline |

- **Rehearse the rollback in staging**, end to end, and time it. An untested rollback is not a rollback.

> **Exit gate:** rollback executed successfully in staging; runbook links, dashboards, and on-call owner published.

## 5. Cut over progressively with bake
